Name: Corrin Lakeland
Question: Do Teslas learn specific roads? If previous Teslas have swerved to avoid a pothole, will other Teslas be aware of it?
Answer: No The idea is that stuff like potholes are too transient. It's better to have a car that can adapt to their presence without advance notice. There is the ability for the cars to learn, but it's much more controlled than that. For example Tesla might observe that they have a lot of complaints about cars mishandling potholes, so they put software on the cars to monitor them and send back pothole footage. Then Tesla train their software using that footage and send out an update.

Question: How can I know which stocks I should invest in?
Answer: here’s only been twice in my life where I was certain what stocks to invest in, and both were frauds where I was an expert in the field and could see through it. That’s over twenty years. Note that even if you know for sure that something is a fraud, to make money you still need enough that the broker doesn’t force your hand before the market catches up with you. The reason it’s hard is that every stock is owned by someone that’s done their homework and believes that stock is worth more. Every stock for sale is someone that’s done their homework and believes the stock will drop. There might be a lot of investors that haven’t done very much homework, but they are all pretty small time. The investors you end up betting against are all professionals that study this stuff all day, every day. To me, that gives two options: stick to private companies that the professionals can’t touch, and/or invest using a formula. Something like an index fund means that rather than picking a stock, you instead by a tiny slice of every single stock in the market and therefore are all-but guaranteed to get the market average performance.

Question: What's the difference between Indigent Care and Universal Health Care?
Answer: Indigent care is a little like food stamps. Some members of the public are able to shop in a private business for free. They’re only allowed to purchase certain products - couldn’t have them using food stamps to buy condoms after all… Universal health care is a little like voting. The government runs it and pays for it, not the people using the service. Sometimes the service is better in some areas than others, and sometimes the service really isn’t good enough. Universal health care covers all citizens, just like all citizens are eligible to vote. Rich or poor, young or old. Universal health care covers most medical treatments: cancer, dialysis, MRIs, etc. If your healthcare professional says you need it then it’s covered. By contrast Indigent care only covers the poor, only covers some services: “Benefits are limited to participating administrators who provide primary, preventative and some specialty services”. Earn a lot of money but are transferring between jobs so don’t have healthcare for a few days? You’d be covered under universal healthcare but not under Indigent care. Broke your leg for the fifteenth time because you won’t give up dangerous sports? You’d be covered under universal healthcare. Really, really want a CT scan but your doctor says no? You can’t get one under universal healthcare - the medical profession prioritises who gets treatment.

Question: If everybody in America switched to an electric vehicle tomorrow, and there were ample charging stations, would the grid be able to handle the load?
Answer: A couple years ago the demand for Tesla was so much higher than supply that some people were selling their year old car for more than they bought it for. EV manufacturers were ramping up production as fast as they could to try and satisfy this demand. During this time, we didn't have too much trouble building charging stations at the rate one per ten thousand cars sold or whatever the actual ratio was. So yes, if everyone woke up tomorrow and said: “you know what, my next car witbe an EV”, we would be able to build charging stations for them before we could deliver the cars. The power usage by electric cars is relatively minor, at around 10kWh per day. It's also conveniently at a time that has historically been a lull in demand. That said, decades of underinvestment in the grid have left it prone to breaking, to the point that even a modest increase in demand could be too much. Since electricity use is clearly going up rather than down, and power plants take many years to build, there is an urgent need to build more now. EVs aren't the problem there much more than say electric toothbrushes, both are basically rounding errors in demand. Also both would be largely unaffected by the odd power cut since they both have enough battery to easily wait for power to come back on. That's not true of AC units, or the laser cutter I just bought at work. We need to build more power plants because otherwise we won't being unable to turn on the AC, manufacture, produce steel, or use LLMs … those things matter regardless of your political persuasion.

Question: Why does a man think of earning money even though he has unlimited money?
Answer: My friend has had enough money to retire ever since I met him. His net worth at the time was around $10m, so invested modestly he could generate an annual income of $400k. He’s one of the hardest workers I know and is a little obsessed about money, always chasing more. Unlike me he has ambitions to increase his net worth significantly and is tackling projects that could double his wealth or bankrupt him. This makes very little sense to me; my focus is always around having enough, and there is virtually no benefit in having more than enough. I really struggle with the idea of risking enough in the pursuit of more. I think there’s two things going on: He went through a most of his adult years trying to grow a business that gradually became worth a lot on paper but wasn’t paying him. His whole adult life until shortly before I met him had required him to actively seek out ways to make money, so he had literal decades of developing this habit. His attitude towards accumulating money is very different to mine. He treats it as part of the game of life and the pursuit of happiness, so if he’s accumulating money then he’s doing well with that facet of his life. Mine is that money buys stability, and once you have that then deeper foundations are pointless - your focus has to shift. Anyway this is obviously sample-of-one stuff and I don’t know how representative he is. I find it useful to remember because it highlights that my attitude towards money is not the only valid option. When I look around at the big projects that happen, I realise both that it’s good many of them happen, and that there is absolutely no circumstance that I would have started that project so the world clearly needs people with different attitudes.

Question: When will electric vehicles be automatically rechargeable?
Answer: Ah yes, the robotic pump, as seen at gas stations across the world. These exist you know, the tech to recharge a car (gas or electric) is the same and it’s been around for years. Give me $20k and I’ll even arrange an installer for you. What’s missing is consumer demand. Would you pay $20k to have your car recharge itself? Would you even pay $2k? Think about what’s needed - A number of servos to hold and move things tidily, and some simple vision to spot where to go. “The cost of a robotic arm varies depending on the type of arm, its capabilities, and the accessories and peripherals needed to operate it. Simple single-axis robots can cost as little as $3,000, while more advanced articulated robots …”. Charging a EV would require movement on two axes, which would put it at around $10k, but it would also benefit from massive economies of scale which I’d guess would make a 10x difference and bring the final price down to $1k eventually. Every technology goes through a phase where early adopters pay a premium, and then everyone else gets it for cheaper. Right now the early adopters are staying away because it’s too expensive. Right now, autonomous charging would save typical owners maybe ten seconds a day and very few people are rich or geeky enough to make that trade. My guess is this will change when parked vehicle summoning becomes much better. Imagine your car coming out from the parking garage and picking you up. Once the tech to achieve this is available, who would want to go into a parking garage ever again? Get dropped off at the entrance and the car sorts out parking. At that point charging goes from being a ten second task to a major inconvenience and my bet is these garages will be the early adopters. I’d give it five years.

Question: Everybody talks about how much they are saving with an electric car. What about the time it take to charge it?
Answer: In the last six months I’ve had to wait for my car to charge twice. The vast majority of the time I plug in when I get home which takes almost no time; the vast majority of the rest of the time I’m on some sort of trip and I coincide recharging the car for when I need a rechard too. The best analogy I have is to imagine that your gas car really didn’t like being filled up twice on the same day. If you need to do that then it can only be done at a mechanic rather than a regular gas station. That’s roughly what it’s like with an EV - a minor waste of time once every blue moon.

Question: How do different financial advisors make a difference to your retirement funds?
Answer: Consider these two alternative strategies: You should own a single rental that you look after yourself, you will save heaps on a property manager plus you will do a better job. Versus You should put your money into an index fund. You'll do well in good years, poorly in bad years, but mostly you'll get average returns Both these strategies have the same expected return (or at least they do in this hypothetical). However one has a small possibility of disaster mixed with a high probability of good returns, while the other has almost a fifty percent chance of a disappointing result Neither option is wrong. The rental might suit someone intending to live off the rent, willing to take the tiny chance on disaster. Index funds might suit someone who can cope with a more variable income. A decent financial advisor will work out what return distribution best suits a client. Plus they'll explain it using language the client understands.

Question: Why does the bank ask my "net worth" when I request to open a new account (saving account)?
Answer: They want to know how much they should wine and dine you. Let’s say you are opening a savings account and putting $5k in, while someone else is also opening a savings account and also putting $5k in… The two of you have a lot in common except you own a $20m company which has accounts at a different bank, while they other guy doesn’t. You’ll get some VIP treatment even though you have minimal assets with the bank because they hope doing so will tempt you to bring more banking to them. The other guy won’t - the bank’s profit on a $5k deposit is maybe $50/year. It’s just not enough to even pay someone to check in on him. I actually did a project not long ago trying to identify customers with investments elsewhere based on their transactional behaviour. It’s not particularly accurate, but then neither is asking people their net worth when they open a new account.

Question: My car, a Toyota Avensis 2010, is making 9.3km/l. Is this a good economy?

You can make the numbers work much better by getting a three or so year old fuel efficient car. Some people do the calculation and use it to justify getting a new EV. That works, but only if you ignore that a three year old car would score better.

Question: Would you rather have $2 million in 1850 or $750K today?
Answer: One of the things I’ve discovered about myself is that I prefer being in a similar position to the people around me. Two million dollars in 1850 is an almost incomprehendible amount of money, enough to live life like a king with a large team of servants. Yet I wouldn’t have a washing machine, fridge, car, phone, computer or any of dozens of modern conveniences. Daily life wouldn’t be so bad with servants looking after your clothes, preparing your meals and your bath… but those things are pretty easy with a washing machine, induction hob, and shower. Have I mentioned healthcare yet? The big thing that puts me off though is that I’d be surrounded by people with far less than me. I’d have to assume that every overture of friendship was someone wanting to get at my wealth, and that I’d be one big screw-up away from a life in the gutter. I like being normal. I live in a country with universal healthcare, a (mostly) decent minimum wage, and loads of free activities such as sports grounds and nature walks. Less than a million dollars today is enough to provide a $30k or so ‘income top-up’. Not quite enough to live off unless you’re really frugal, but enough to turn a regular job into a comfortable life. More important is that I’d be hardly worse off if I somehow lost the money. Also the $750k would barely be visible between me and people I interacted with. It seems an easy choice.

Question: I want to earn $50k a year in salary or business. What should I study right now or how can I start?
Answer: Business is not a smart way to earn a target like $50k. Most businesses lose money in their first years, and in subsequent years are highly variable. A business averaging a net profit of $50k could well have returns of $120k, -$20k, $30k, $70k. Go into business because you're passionate about it. Set it up so it returns enough money. But don't do it with the primary goal of earning an average salary. A waged job is a far easier and safer route to achieve that. My experience is that cool, exciting jobs have more people wanting to get into them than boring essential jobs. The plumbers of the world will always be in demand, both literally and figuratively.

Question: How many miles does one hour of charging produce for the Tesla Model 3?

Question: What do you think about people using food stamps to buy fresh seafood?
Answer: There’s two ways to answer this: pragmatic and moral. From a pragmatic perspective, every attempt to artificially affect the market always backfires. Food stamps that can’t buy certain groceries will push up the cost of what they can buy and down the cost of what they can’t. Further the admin required to enforce that is nightmarish, can you imagine the software system which goes ‘ah nope, transaction contains seafood, so we must reject that payment’. What you’ll end up with is the large supermarkets supporting it and the smaller grocers saying ‘that’s too hard’, so effectively the person is banned from the smaller, cheaper grocers. The closest I’ve come to experiencing this firsthand was when I was an undergrad at uni. The government decided students might take their student loan and I don’t know… spend it on hookers or something, so they stopped giving out money and instead only allowed you to buy from the university bookstore. As a consequence I had to spend $1k on textbooks rather than maybe $200 buying second-hand. Morally, how does limiting what can be bought make the world a better place? I guess you’re worrying the person will buy expensive seafood and then not have enough money to eat, requiring a second handout? If someone is eligible for support then how about trusting that they work out what’s best for them. Maybe a little treat of seafood is how they maintain sanity in their life? I find the pragmatic argument is more effective when talking with conservatives. They seem to ‘get’ that the government bureaucracy will screw up any guard rails and that the free market will be more efficient, whereas I find arguing that gifts should be unconditional to be ineffective.

Question: How do I save $1k+ per year (while earning minimum wage)?

Question: You have a choice between two EVs. They are the same size and have the same specs except one has a range of 150 mile and costs $20k. The other has a range of 280 miles and costs $35k. Which would you purchase if you had to choose?
Answer: Which would you purchase if you had to choose? I hate artificial choices. In the real world, I have a choice of several dozen EVs. I also have the choice of waiting a few more months when many more EVs will be available. Your question pretty much is “Should I buy a Nissan Leaf or a BYD Atto 3”. There are people for whom the Leaf is the better choice, people for whom the BYD is better, and many people that wouldn’t be happy with either. In my personal case, I drive over 150 miles every month or two. I’d now have to swap cars with my wife for those trips which would be annoying but we’d manage. I almost never drive over 280 miles, and I’m happy to stop and charge mid-journey for something that rare. So if there was nothing different about the cars then I’d go for the cheaper one. It serves my day-to-day needs, and a once every month-or-two hassle isn’t worth an extra $15k. In the real world though, the BYD has far more boot space than the Leaf. It’s got more height and is generally more comfortable to drive. If I was choosing between the BYD for $35k and the Leaf for $20k, I’d go for the BYD because I take the dogs to the park every week and that’d be a pain in the Leaf.

Question: What percentage of your wealth should be spent when buying a car in cash?
Answer: The phrasing of this question is really weird. If you spend more than you earn then you'll quickly end up broke no matter how much you start with. Let me try and give a more realistic example: Gen is a solo mom. She finally dumped her boyfriend after he would never contribute fairly to household chores. Fortunately she has a $2m trust fund to live off. Gen decides she needs a new car to get her kids to daycare, do the shopping and go to dance class. Being the analytical sort, she works out she spends five hours a week in the car out of 112 awake hours and so the car should get about five percent of her income. With two million in her trust fund she will get a stipend of $80k per year. From this she first has to pay tax and health insurance 1/3 which leaves her $53k. Five percent of that is $2650 but note this also has to cover car insurance and maintenance so leaving maybe $1500/year. Gen can therefore afford a $7500 car every five years. She pays cash of course, and it happens to be about 0.25% of her wealth.

Question: How is AI killing software engineers? What can we do to stop it?

Advertise the practice as ‘strictly no men’ and you’ll get women who want a break from guys, as well as women who have weird controlling partners. As much as your question strikes me as weird, I can imagine random weird guys asking similar ones: “My wife is beautiful. I don’t like the idea of her ever being in a room with a man unless I’m there, so how can she go to the dentist?” There are a few ‘women only’ businesses around. I was looking at a taxi service the other day in response to someone whose Uber driver kept hitting on her. It’s an odd niche and excluding half the population is always going to be dubious from a business perspective, but the key for business is to be the best provider of the service for enough customers rather than appealing to everyone. One complication your wife would have is that most good patients come from referrals. With only seeing women you’ve not just eliminated half the potential customers but more important, you’ve effectively eliminated half the potential referrals. This means the practice will have half the growth rate. Note, I’m assuming she is setting up a brand new practice which she’ll own. I can’t imagine any employer tolerating this, or any existing practice surviving the change.

Question: What’s having a Tesla like?
Answer: After the first couple weeks where it is novel… it's a car. You use it to go places, just like whatever car you had before. Never stopping to refuel is nice. Numerous times in the past I was running late for something and ended up ten minutes later. Trips away require slightly more planning, such as checking the place I'm staying has a charger, or finding a supercharger near a nice breakfast place. I like the minimalist interior. I wish it had a HUD (I've ordered a third party one but it's not here yet). I wish there was a button to open the frunk. I think the flat door handles are a gimmick with no benefit. The interior is spacious. I'm still kicking myself for adding a roof rack rather than a tow bar. The cruise control is probably the best part. Driving is substantially less mental energy. OTA updates constantly make the car a little better. Being able to remotely see around the car and getting video footage of any near miss is awesome. The car stopping for every red light or disabled traffic light is really annoying but not quite annoying enough that I've disabled stopping for red. The hill assist and park assist is noticably better than other cars. Summon has the potential to be great but in practice rarely delivers. I love not having services any more. With my old car I felt like I was gambling; sometimes the service would say nothing is wrong and other times they would say that'll be $2,000. Overall I'd say: 75% — it's a car. 10% — EVs are far more convenient than ICE 5% — the exclusively EV manufacturers are better than the old guard 10% — Tesla specifically is good. That's why I have trouble getting excited about a debate on Tesla vs Rivian or similar, at most you're debating the last ten percent.

Question: What are some tips to manage personal finance better?
Answer: The big thing for me was a mindset shift. I’d always viewed budgeting as spending less and depriving myself. A bit like ‘eat your greens’, I’d viewed it as spending on the things I should be buying at the expense of things that I wanted to buy. The shift was to eliminate savings, and instead budget on spending money in the future. Now I wasn’t choosing between ‘saving’ vs ‘grabbing some quick food on the way home so I don’t have to cook’ , but instead between ‘going on a winter holiday’ vs ‘grabbing some quick food on the way home so I don’t have to cook’. This is big, because it means the purpose of spending money is now to enjoy myself, to “create beautiful memories”… I’m deliberately not spending on that quick meal because I think I’ll get more out of something else.

Question: If you were about to start your dream career at 29 with no kids, less than $5000 in debt, and a tax free salary of $140,000 CDN: what would you do to become financially successful long term? (Will be starting a 4 year contract, looking for advice)
Answer: At 29 I wanted to be a university professor. You get to teach and research fascinating things all day, be surrounded by loads of bright people, and the pay is plenty to support a family. That's not a career I'd describe as financially successful. The two ways of being financially successful long term are having enough money invested to live off, or skills that remain in demand (nice to be around, productive). I'm not sure which of these is more important so perhaps work towards both? The other key point, at least for me, is keeping your expenses low. If you cook, do your own maintenance, and don't need much space, then you'll have more than enough money at a much lower income. I remember feeling like a millionaire as a student when I got a stipend AND paid for tutoring.

Question: How does EvGo compare with Tesla's superchargers?
Answer: Firstly I’d like to highlight Steve Baker’s excellent answer. There’s three downsides to third party charges that I’ve noticed: This is mostly Tesla’s fault but they are not integrated into the GPS. If you navigate somewhere and need a charge then it won’t go via a third party charger. This is particularly annoying when a third party charger is simply the only option. Related to this, your car won’t precondition the battery when you’re approaching a third-party fast charger. This makes the first five minutes of charging almost useless. Tesla already has my credit card details and it auto-detects my car. Third party chargers require me to launch a special app, choose the charger and click start. Perhaps it only takes a minute but it’s still annoying. The failure rate of third party chargers is (anecdotally) far worse. I’ve had a charger where I’ve rocked up only to see that it’s reporting a fault. I’ve had several that I simply couldn’t get to work and had to notify the company. I’ve had one that was behind scaffolding so it might be fine but nobody could use it. I’ve had several where they just assumed you’d have your own charging cables. I’ve never had an issue with Tesla chargers.
